A reference book usually earns trust by being selective. This one does the opposite: all 64 hexagrams, all 384 lines, each one run through the same seven sections, in the same order, at the same depth.

That uniformity looks mechanical. It is the point.

## The seven sections

1. **Base text** — the received hexagram and line statements, with 帛书 variants kept where they differ.
2. **Social background** — the conditions the hexagram was written inside: who was fighting whom, what the Zhou court needed, what a line about 田 or 婚媾 actually referred to.
3. **Character exegesis** — the key character of the hexagram traced to its seal form and its pre-Qin usage. 需 is not "wait" in the modern sense; it is waiting with provisions. 訟 is not "argument"; it is a dispute brought to a third party.
4. **Line-by-line reading** — each of the six lines, with 老庄 cross-references where the vocabulary overlaps.
5. **Structural relations** — 综卦, 错卦, 互卦. The hexagram as a position in a field rather than a snapshot.
6. **合与和** — whether this hexagram's coherence comes from unification or from placement.
7. **Common misreadings** — the two or three readings that circulate most widely, and what in the text rules them out.

## Why the same structure every time

Two reasons, one editorial and one intellectual.

The editorial one is comparability. If 乾 gets six pages of exegesis and 井 gets two paragraphs, the book becomes a collection of essays rather than a reference. A reader who wants to know what 井 says about 改邑不改井 should be able to find the same kind of answer they got for 乾, in the same place, with the same layers.

The intellectual one is that the seven sections are not seven topics; they are seven checks on the same claim. Take any line and assert a reading. Does the base text support it? Does the social background make it plausible? Does the character's pre-Qin usage allow it? Do the neighboring lines constrain it? Does the inverted hexagram contradict it? Is the coherence 合 or 和? Has someone already read it this way, and why is that reading wrong?

A reading that survives all seven is not proven, but it is accountable. That is the difference between exegesis and opinion.

## The structural sections do the most work

Of the seven, sections 4 and 5 are where most readings fail.

Failing section 4 usually means the reader has treated a line as a standalone proverb. But a line's meaning is constrained by the line below and the line above: 九三 is dangerous because 九二 already succeeded; 上六 is stranded because 九五 has already committed. Read one line alone and you will read it wrong, however well you know the character.

Failing section 5 means ignoring that no hexagram is alone. Read 泰 upside down and you get 否 — the same six lines, opposite reading. The text is telling you that prosperity and blockage are the same structure seen from two ends. Read every line flipped and you get 否's opposite, which is often the condition the original depends on. Read the inner lines and you find another hexagram nested inside the first.

This is why the Yizhuan can mark position without issuing verdicts: it has enough structure to locate a line without needing to grade it.

## What the uniformity is not

It is not a claim that all hexagrams are equally important, or that the same seven sections produce equal depth. Some hexagrams carry two pages of social background; some carry six. The frame is fixed, the content is not.

It is also not an attempt to flatten disagreement. Where 王弼, the 正义, the 本义 and the 集解 diverge, the main text follows one and the notes keep the others; where the 帛书 differs and the evidence doesn't decide, both stand.

## Numbers

72 卷, 50.5 万 characters, v1.50.0, 704-page print PDF. The structured data — hexagram, line, layer, base text, variant, source — is also published as a dataset, so a reading can be checked line by line rather than trusted page by page.
